records.statement: Coin is spoken of as white (silver) and red (gold).

records.statement: Clement advises Ralph to serve the abbot as a man of war.

records.statement: Apart from such pools the downs are waterless.

records.statement: Clement holds plenty of this year's down fleeces; Upmeads cannot raise such wool.

records.statement: They have no lord or master, are unlettered, and seldom enter a church.

records.statement: Summoning signal: a great fire on each corner of the top wall of Bear Castle and the watchword "Smite aside the axe, O Bear-father".

records.statement: Hot day with a south-west wind on the downs.

records.statement: Her wine is good island wine.

records.statement: Townsfolk include burgesses and vavassors.

records.statement: It is midsummer after haysel.
records.subject: Higham-on-the-Way

records.statement: The monk says the wood holds lawless men who have forgotten hell, and worse wights besides.

records.statement: Some men of the house read heathen sages and Church doctors and make books for scribes to copy.

refs.q: took a gold crown from his pouch

records.subject: Ralph

records.subject: Higham-on-the-Way

records.statement: Countryfolk bring food and wares into the town and Abbey.
records.subject: Higham-on-the-Way

records.statement: The by-word of the wood's outlaws is "Thou shalt lack ere I lack".
records.subject: Wood Perilous

records.statement: Hillsides of vineyards and orchards; dales of corn.
records.subject: (unnamed) vine country south of Higham

records.statement: The country people are well clad, unhurried and unafraid.

records.statement: The tavern serves bread, flesh and wine of the hillside.

records.statement: Chapmen ride to the Burg in large companies for safety.

for we have many foes in the wildwood

records.statement: Hares, a hart and hinds feed near the crossroads at evening.

records.statement: Felled oaks have regrown as coppice: evidence of woodcutting in the forest.

records.statement: She expects the Burg folk would mock anyone asking the way to the Well.

records.statement: They ride well horsed and shoot Turk bows from horseback.

records.statement: Roger says the Dry Tree has many women like her, so the Queen herself is hard to take.

records.statement: Houses stout, plain, neither poor nor lordly; folk dark and low, plainly but stoutly clad.

records.statement: Most men carry weapons and staves and wear short brown or blue jerkins, ready for battle.

records.statement: Captive women are sold at the market-cross to the highest bidder; fair young ones fetch a good price.
records.subject: Wheat-wearers

records.statement: All Wheat-wearer males taken are slain, by ancient oath; Dry Tree carles taken are also slain.

records.statement: Wheat-wearer thrall women are good weavers of figured silk.
records.subject: Wheat-wearers

refs.q: did we make the Burg strong and hard to win, as ye see it to-day

records.subject: Burg of the Four Friths

records.statement: By the War-smith's order all freemen learn war; women, thralls and aliens do other crafts and trade.
records.subject: Burg of the Four Friths

records.subject: Fellowship of the Dry Tree

refs.q: because sorcery goes with them, and the wiles of one who is their Queen

records.statement: Sorcery and the wiles of their Queen make them hard to crush.
records.subject: Fellowship of the Dry Tree

records.statement: The burgher says conquering them outright would mean endless fighting, so the Burg raids instead.
records.subject: Wheat-wearers

records.statement: Strangers who neither serve nor trade are viewed with suspicion.

records.statement: Warders on the walls challenge and call the hours; the belfry chimes.

records.statement: He shoots two arrows in quick succession, each felling a man.

records.statement: Ralph is lodged as master and Roger as man.

records.statement: They rarely go into the wood beyond sight of open daylight and never beyond it.

records.statement: She sits in the chamber of estate to hear cases and give judgements.

refs.q: which had not been shrouded these eight years

records.subject: Knight of the Sun

refs.q: thou art strong-armed as well as white-armed

records.statement: She is strong-armed enough to hold the Knight's dagger hand.
records.subject: (unnamed) lady delivered at the crossroads

refs.q: it must be this hand, and the learning which it hath learned which must deal with him for a while

records.statement: She dresses Walter's side wound; the Knight calls her a good leech; she says only her hand and learning can save him.
records.subject: (unnamed) lady delivered at the crossroads

refs.q: ye may not heal this man so that he may sit in his saddle within these ten days

records.statement: The Knight says Walter cannot ride within ten days.
records.subject: Walter the Black

refs.q: took from them bread and flesh, and a flask of good wine

records.statement: His saddle-bags hold bread, flesh and a flask of wine.
records.subject: Walter the Black

refs.q: thou art my prisoner, to be kept or ransomed, or set free as I will

records.statement: A prisoner may be kept, ransomed or freed at the captor's will.
records.subject: Knight of the Sun

refs.q: took hold of the two fingers of her left hand with her right forefinger, and let the thumb meet it, so that it made a circle about them

records.statement: She forms a ring with her fingers and murmurs; soon after, the wished-for holy man arrives.
records.subject: (unnamed) lady delivered at the crossroads

refs.q: I heard the thornbushes speaking to me like men

records.statement: The friar says thornbushes spoke to him like men and sent him to help someone in need.
records.subject: (unnamed) Blackfriar hermit of the lake

refs.q: from her hands goeth all healing, as it was with the holy men of old time

records.statement: The friar says all healing goes from her hands, like the holy men of old.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: thou swayest man and beast in the wildwood

records.statement: The Knight says men say she sways man and beast in the wildwood.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: maybe as long as either of you twain

records.statement: The lady says Walter may live as long as either of the two men.
records.subject: Walter the Black

refs.q: bread and other meat, and milk of my goats

records.statement: He keeps goats and has bread at his cell.
records.subject: (unnamed) Blackfriar hermit of the lake

refs.q: he made a tale of me of true and false mingled, that I was a wise-wife and an enchantress

records.statement: Walter told a tale, true and false mingled, that she was a wise-wife and enchantress; she was shamed and driven out barefoot and bleeding.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: he will not slay any man for my sake

records.statement: The Captain of the Dry Tree desires her "as others have", but would not kill for her.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: the broken doom-ring of a forgotten folk

records.statement: A broken stone ring in the forest is likened to a doom-ring (court circle) of a forgotten folk.
records.subject: the ancient folk

refs.q: I said a word in the ear of Silverfax or ever I departed, and now the good beast knows my mind

records.statement: The Lady says she whispered in Silverfax's ear so the horse will lead her husband a little astray.
records.subject: Silverfax

refs.q: in my knowing of these woods, there is no sorcery at all

records.statement: She says her knowledge of the woods is no sorcery: she was bred in woods.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: if he come, he will be by himself alone

records.statement: The Lady says he would never gather folk to chase one man; he would come alone.
records.subject: Knight of the Sun

refs.q: went hither and thither gathering strawberries about the bank

records.statement: Wild strawberries grow along the bank in June.
records.subject: (unnamed) strawberry brook

refs.q: light-foot as the Wood-wife and Goddess of yore agone
even Diana, the Wood-wife of yore agone

records.statement: She compares herself to the Wood-wife and Goddess of old, Diana.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: the shuttle was flying from side to side, and the shed opening and changing

records.statement: A loom wove by itself while she sat naked singing from a great book in a storm.
records.subject: (unnamed) witch-mistress of the Lady

refs.q: dipped her fingers in the blood and reddened both herself and me on the breast, and the hands, and the feet

records.statement: She sacrificed the white goat on the stone table, marked the girl and herself with blood, burned it on seven faggots and sang.
records.subject: (unnamed) witch-mistress of the Lady

refs.q: something must be slain and offered up here on this altar, lest all come to naught

records.statement: She says something must be offered on the altar "lest all come to naught".
records.subject: (unnamed) witch-mistress of the Lady

refs.q: she made fire, but I saw not how

records.statement: She lit the fire, but the girl did not see how.
records.subject: (unnamed) witch-mistress of the Lady

refs.q: the wild things, even to the conies and fawns loved me

records.statement: Wild creatures loved her and did not fear her.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: Here, then, is another seeker who hath not found

records.statement: The witch calls the dead woman "another seeker who hath not found".
records.subject: Well at the World's End

refs.q: Nought else I knew save how to spin, and to tend our goats and milk them, and to set snares

records.statement: The girl spun flax or hair, herded and milked goats, snared birds and small deer, and slept among the goats.
records.subject: (unnamed) witch's forest house

refs.q: be before the wolves

records.statement: Wolves roam the forest in winter.
records.subject: (unnamed) witch's forest house

refs.q: the only thing in all the wood wherein I was used to wander which was of man's handiwork

records.statement: The stone table was the only man-made thing in the wood apart from the house.
records.subject: (unnamed) yew ring and stone table

refs.q: henceforth no man who seeth thee once will forget thee ever, or cease to long for thee: of a surety this is thy weird

records.statement: The carline foretells as her fate (weird) that no man who sees her will forget her or stop longing for her.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: thou hast not yet drunk of the Well at the World's End

records.statement: The witch says the girl has not drunk of the Well and cannot escape her reach while she lives.
records.subject: (unnamed) witch-mistress of the Lady

refs.q: I learned like a little lad in the chorister's school

records.statement: She teaches the girl letters "like a little lad in the chorister's school".
records.subject: Teacher of Lore

refs.q: I tied my goatskin shoes to my feet

records.statement: As a thrall she wore rough cloth and goatskin shoes.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: for fear that some spell might get to work in them if they were opened

records.statement: The girl feared spells might work if the books were opened.
records.subject: (unnamed) three great books of the witch

refs.q: made curds thereof with the woodland roots

records.statement: She lives on goats' milk, curds made with woodland roots, and berries.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: in the Well at the World's End is no evil, but only the Quenching of Sorrow, and Clearing of the Eyes that they may behold

records.statement: The Lady says the Well holds no evil but the Quenching of Sorrow and Clearing of the Eyes; her long life and beauty come from it.
records.subject: Well at the World's End

refs.q: the said book was made not by my friends but my foes

records.statement: The Lady says the book was made by her foes, partly false on purpose and partly confused.
records.subject: (unnamed) book of the Well

refs.q: were heathen, as the Gentiles of yore agone

records.statement: They are heathen, without knowledge of the Church, and revere their fathers of old.
records.subject: (unnamed) heathen simple folk beyond the mountains

refs.q: we went our ways from them riding on horned neat

records.statement: They have no horses and ride horned cattle; they gave bows and arrows.
records.subject: (unnamed) heathen simple folk beyond the mountains

refs.q: Not that the way was long, as I found out afterwards, but that we went astray in the woodland

records.statement: The way was not long but they strayed; they crossed the stony waste on the fourth try with food from her woodcraft.
records.subject: (unnamed) dreadful stony waste

refs.q: whereas they were not of his foes (who lay for the more part on the other side of his land)

records.statement: The king's foes lay mostly on the far side of his land.
records.subject: (unnamed) kingdom of the king's son

refs.q: a happy abode for the tillers of the soil, and the fashioners of wares

records.statement: It was a peaceful land of tillers and craftsmen in those days.
records.subject: (unnamed) kingdom of the king's son

refs.q: I was brought in guilty of sorcery, and doomed to be burned in the Great Square in three days time

records.statement: The Lady was tried by the king's bishops for sorcery and sentenced to burn.
records.subject: Kingdom of the Tower

refs.q: the Bishop bore in his hand the Blessed Host

records.statement: A Bishop bearing the Host and the Abbot of St. Peter's with monks halted the battle.
records.subject: Kingdom of the Tower

refs.q: it endured year after year, till fighting became the chief business of all in the land

records.statement: War between father and son lasted year after year until fighting was the land's chief business.
records.subject: Kingdom of the Tower

refs.q: we robbed no poor folk and needy, but rewarded them rather

records.statement: As outlaws they robbed only rich men, lords and hard chapmen and protected tillers, yet got a name as devils and witches.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: their fierceness was and is but kindness and pity when set against the cruelty of the Burg of the Four Friths

records.statement: The Lady calls the Dry Tree's fierceness kindness beside the cruelty of the Burg.
records.subject: Fellowship of the Dry Tree

refs.q: I promised them and swore to them by the Water of the Well at the World's End

records.statement: She swore by the Water of the Well to return to the Dry Tree as their Lady, setting no date.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: The dead may not drink of the Well at the World's End; yet the living may, even if they be old

records.statement: The Teacher says the dead cannot drink of the Well, but the living, even the old, can, and are young again for a long while.
records.subject: Teacher of Lore

refs.q: it was no hard matter for her to give me another semblance than mine own

records.statement: She could give the Lady another appearance so none knew her.
records.subject: Teacher of Lore

refs.q: as the foreseeing of things to come, and the sending of dreams or visions

records.statement: She learned foreseeing, sending dreams or visions and other things called sorcery; she sent the friar his dream.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: as though some foretaste of the Well was there for us in the loneliness of the desert

records.statement: In the desert house she grew no older, and stronger, "as though some foretaste of the Well was there".
records.subject: House of the Sorceress

refs.q: sent by the lords of hell to wreck that fair Land of the Tower

records.statement: Women especially blamed the Lady; tales said she was sent from hell to wreck the land.
records.subject: Kingdom of the Tower

refs.q: a pestilence that war and famine had brought upon the land

records.statement: War and famine brought pestilence.
records.subject: Kingdom of the Tower

refs.q: we had before that dwelt at a little manor house that was there

records.statement: A little manor house stood there before the castle was built; it was a refuge during the war.
records.subject: House of Abundance

refs.q: each of us signed and marked out for the quest by bearing such-like beads as thou and I both bear upon our necks today

records.statement: Seekers wore bead necklaces like those Ralph and the Lady wear, marking them for the quest.
records.subject: Well at the World's End

refs.q: my youth was renewed in me, and I became as thou seest me to-day

records.statement: Drinking renewed the Lady's youth; the Teacher became like a woman of forty.
records.subject: Well at the World's End

refs.q: Fifty years ago, when I was yet but a young man

records.statement: Geoffrey says it was fifty years since the Queen vanished.
records.subject: Kingdom of the Tower

refs.q: in the Great City are but few people, grass grows in its streets

records.statement: The Land of the Tower is ruined by folly, war and greed; grass grows in the Great City's streets and merchants avoid it.
records.subject: Kingdom of the Tower

refs.q: there is none so great as the Burg in all the lands about

records.statement: The Burg has thriven greatly and is the greatest power in the lands about.
records.subject: Burg of the Four Friths

refs.q: They are warriors and champions from father to son; therefore have they thriven not over well

records.statement: They are warriors from father to son and have not thriven much.
records.subject: Fellowship of the Dry Tree

refs.q: they loved me, yet it was with fear

records.statement: The folk of Abundance honour the Lady like a saint but with fear.
records.subject: yeomen of Abundance

refs.q: they had naught but white gaberdines over their hauberks, with no coat-armour or token upon them

records.statement: The seekers wore white gaberdines over hauberks with no coat-armour or token.
records.subject: Fellowship of the Dry Tree

refs.q: there have I dwelt ever since betwixt Hampton and the Castle of Abundance

records.statement: After being cast out she went with the tall champion to Hampton and has lived between Hampton and the Castle of Abundance.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: I foresaw not, any more than I can foresee to-morrow

records.statement: She says she cannot foresee everything; she only knew they must pass this way and stored food.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: which was an easy thing to me, so much as I had learned

records.statement: She led the prisoner past all gates and guards, an easy thing for her with what she had learned.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: I use my wisdom which I have learned, to set free luckless wights from her anger and malice

records.statement: Some ill deeds told of the Lady were the older Queen's doing; the Lady secretly frees those she condemns.
records.subject: (unnamed) old Queen of the Dry Tree

refs.q: the Well at the World's End, which quencheth all sorrow

records.statement: The maiden calls the Well the thing that quenches all sorrow.
records.subject: Well at the World's End

refs.q: who had been haled before our old Queen for a spy and doomed by her

records.statement: The maiden was judged a spy by the old Queen and would be slain.
records.subject: Fellowship of the Dry Tree

refs.q: it was once one of the fairest of lands, with castles and cots and homesteads all about

records.statement: The Lady thinks it was once one of the fairest lands, with castles, cots and homesteads; the tales of its wasting blend with the War of the Tower.
records.subject: (unnamed) sandstone desert

refs.q: they saw plenteous deer both great and small, and the wild things seemed to fear them but little

records.statement: Deer of all sizes are plentiful and fear people little; few hunters or wayfarers pass.
records.subject: (unnamed) sandstone desert

refs.q: shoot well, all woodcraft comes handy to me

records.statement: She says she shoots well and keeps a bow, arrows, kettle, meal and wine stored in the cave.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: had turned the bezels of her finger-rings outward, for joy of that meeting

records.statement: For the meeting she wore meadowsweet and eglantine and turned her ring-bezels outward.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: let his bones be covered up from the wolf and the kite

records.statement: Ralph buries the Lady in the cave and raises a separate cairn over her slayer, against wolves and kites.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: he smote a roe with a shaft and slew her

records.statement: Ralph shoots a roe for food in the valley thicket.
records.subject: (unnamed) sandstone desert

refs.q: merchants clad goodly, with three carles, their servants

records.statement: Travellers include armed merchants with armed servants and country women carrying produce by ass.
records.subject: (unnamed) road across the downs

refs.q: there were carts and sheds scattered about the hither side, and sheep and neat feeding in the meadows

records.statement: The valley is peopled: carts, sheds, sheep and cattle in the meadows.
records.subject: (unnamed) sheep downs by the Swelling Flood

refs.q: like some lord's man going a message

records.statement: A lord's messenger rides with jack, sallet, long spear and saddle budgets.
records.subject: (unnamed) road across the downs

refs.q: the Companions who had conquered it were looking for chapmen to cheapen their booty

records.statement: Companions who had taken a rich town sold the booty cheaply to the first buyers; Blaise resold it at profit from town to town.
records.subject: Blaise

refs.q: he and other chapmen had armed them, and waged men-at-arms to defend them, and so tried the adventure of the wildwoods

records.statement: Merchants arm themselves and hire men-at-arms to cross the wildwoods.
records.subject: (unnamed) merchant company to Whitwall

refs.q: I have had good hap in these days, though scarce kingly or knightly, for I have been buying and selling

records.statement: Blaise says trading is "scarce kingly or knightly", but few know Upmeads to blame him.
records.subject: Blaise

refs.q: men-at-arms good store to garnish them

records.statement: Whitwall's high new walls are well manned.
records.subject: Whitwall

refs.q: since the blossom-tide of Whitwall was not many years old

records.statement: Whitwall's prosperity is recent; its church is new.
records.subject: Whitwall

refs.q: for it was a land of many waters

records.statement: The country around is a land of many waters.
records.subject: Whitwall

refs.q: he held that such a quest came of the inspiration of the devils, and was but a memory of the customs of the ancient gentiles and heathen

records.statement: He held the Well-quest to be inspired by devils and a remnant of heathen custom.
records.subject: Sir Cyprian

refs.q: they went afoot crowned with flowers, and the pipe and tabour playing before them

records.statement: They set out on foot crowned with flowers, pipe and tabour before them, with a pack ass.
records.subject: (unnamed) three Swevenham seekers

refs.q: a thing to be sought, which should cure sorrow, and make life blossom in the old, and uphold life in the young

records.statement: Swevenham tales say the Well cures sorrow, makes life blossom in the old and upholds it in the young.
records.subject: Well at the World's End

refs.q: to-morrow is Saturday, and high market in Whitwall

records.statement: Saturday is high market in Whitwall; country folk come in.
records.subject: Whitwall

refs.q: they have already bidden him to the freedom of the city

records.statement: Whitwall offers Blaise the freedom of the city.
records.subject: Blaise

refs.q: was but of eighteen winters, who am now of three score and eight

records.statement: Richard is sixty-eight; he was eighteen when the seekers left.
records.subject: Richard the Red

refs.q: paid him due scot for the passage of the Wood

records.statement: Merchants pay the Dry Tree's Bailiff a toll to pass the Wood.
records.subject: Fellowship of the Dry Tree

refs.q: pieces of good and fine cloth plumbed with the seal of the greatest of the cities

records.statement: Blaise's booth holds fine cloth sealed by the greatest cities, Babylon silk, island spices, silver and gold work, and fine arms.
records.subject: Blaise

refs.q: a rumour that they had lost their young Queen and Lady

records.statement: Rumour of the loss of their young Queen will make them fierce; their old Queen still lives.
records.subject: Fellowship of the Dry Tree

refs.q: whiles have been slain by the champions, whiles have entered their company

records.statement: Seekers of the Well must pass the Dry Tree; some are misled to Hampton and slain or recruited.
records.subject: Dry Tree

refs.q: hast seen three very fair cities, besides towns and castles and thorps and strange men, and fair merchandize

records.statement: Clement's eastern route passes three fair cities, towns, castles and thorps.
records.subject: Clement Chapman

refs.q: a sign hung out of the fruitful tree by the water-side

records.statement: Blaise uses the Upmeads arms (fruitful tree by water) as his shop sign.
records.subject: Blaise

refs.q: this is but the image of me as thou hast known me

records.statement: The dead Lady appears in a dream, saying it is but her image, and cannot tell the way to the Well.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: I am a sending of the woman whom thou hast loved

records.statement: The vision of the maiden says she is a sending of the woman Ralph loved.
records.subject: Ursula

refs.q: for it was market-day, and the country folk were early afoot

records.statement: On market day country folk arrive early with herbs, worts and fruit.
records.subject: Whitwall

refs.q: he who could lay his hand on the bole thereof was like enough to drink of the Well at the World's End

records.statement: Whoever lays hand on the Dry Tree's bole is likely to drink of the Well (one old man's claim).
records.subject: Dry Tree

refs.q: a woman had brought the tidings thereof to those valiant men, and had fixed the name upon them

records.statement: Rumour says a woman brought word of the Dry Tree to the Hampton champions and fixed the name on them.
records.subject: Fellowship of the Dry Tree

refs.q: Twenty years agone a great sickness lay heavy upon us and the folk of Whitwall

records.statement: Twenty years ago a great sickness struck Swevenham and Whitwall; five young men left to seek the Well's water and never returned.
records.subject: Swevenham

refs.q: two knights riding east from Whitwall

records.statement: Two knights riding east from Whitwall asked the road to the Well.
records.subject: Swevenham

refs.q: From ruin and wrack to the Well at the World's End

records.statement: A woman with a gem chaplet on the east highway said she went "from ruin and wrack to the Well" and drew a sword on would-be robbers.
records.subject: Well at the World's End

refs.q: From unrest to the Well at the World's End.

records.statement: Five days ago a slender woman rider with a chaplet and an anlace said she went "from unrest to the Well".
records.subject: Well at the World's End

refs.q: the book tells concerning the Dry Tree, and of kings sitting in their chairs in the mountains nearby

records.statement: The book tells of the Dry Tree and kings sitting in their chairs in nearby mountains.
records.subject: (unnamed) book of Alexander

refs.q: when he is whole again, we may look for him at our gates

records.statement: Whitwall expects war with Earl Walter once he heals; it will expect knightly service of Ralph.
records.subject: Whitwall

refs.q: there was some blending in her of the blood of the fays

records.statement: Richard guesses the Lady was not wholly human but had some blood of the fays.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: I deem both that the Well verily is, and that thou thyself shalt find it

records.statement: Having heard Ralph's tale, Richard now believes the Well is real and that Ralph will find it.
records.subject: Well at the World's End

refs.q: the cupboard was of five shelves as was but meet for a king's son

records.statement: Blaise's cupboard of plate has five shelves, "meet for a king's son".
records.subject: Blaise

refs.q: the way is long, and our goods worth the lifting

records.statement: Clement rides armed in a coat of proof and sallet; the road has rough places and robbers.
records.subject: Clement Chapman

refs.q: or are ruled by the customs of the manor, or by due lawful Earls and Kings, or the laws of the Lineage or the Port, or have any Guilds

records.statement: Whitwall is the last land with courtesy, manor custom, lawful earls and kings, laws of the Lineage or Port, and guilds.
records.subject: Whitwall

refs.q: as swearing on the altars of devils, and eating horse-flesh at the High-tides, and spell-raising more than enough

records.statement: Nominally Christian but with heathen customs: oaths on devils' altars, eating horse-flesh at high feasts, spell-raising, and blood (even of babes) on the doom-rings.
records.subject: (unnamed) eastern tyrant lands

refs.q: merely masterful and wise men who have gained their place by cunning and the high hand

records.statement: Towns are ruled by self-made tyrants of no great kindred who won power by cunning and force.
records.subject: (unnamed) eastern tyrant lands

refs.q: their tillers and shepherds and workmen and servants be mere thralls, whom they may sell at any market

records.statement: Tillers, shepherds and workers are thralls sold at market; free men must serve some tyrant by bow and sword.
records.subject: (unnamed) eastern tyrant lands

refs.q: these lands be fruitful of wine and oil and wheat, and neat and sheep; withal metals and gems are dug up out of the mountains

records.statement: Rich in wine, oil, wheat, cattle and sheep; metals and gems are mined from the mountains; few crafts, so eager for merchants.
records.subject: (unnamed) eastern tyrant lands

refs.q: that house is hallowed unto truce, and no man smiteth another therein

records.statement: The house is hallowed to truce: no one strikes another there; departing foes get an hour's grace.
records.subject: Mid-Mountain House

refs.q: with less than a score of men well-armed the danger of death or captivity is over great

records.statement: Fewer than a score of armed men risk death or capture on the mountain road.
records.subject: (unnamed) entry of the mountains

refs.q: a house, long and low, builded of great stones, both walls and roof

records.statement: Long and low, walls and roof of great stones, with a garth gate.
records.subject: Mid-Mountain House

refs.q: doth a man make a hole in a piece of cloth which he is taking to market?

records.statement: Thieves keep captives in foot-shackles, treat them well as goods for market.
records.subject: Strong-thieves of the mountains

refs.q: a few beeves driven into our garth; a pack or two brought into the hall

records.statement: Thieves bring beeves, packs and captives through the House.
records.subject: Strong-thieves of the mountains

refs.q: I shall look on it as a token that they are about waylaying us if we come on none of them in the Mountain House

records.statement: Clement reads an empty House as a sign the thieves plan an ambush.
records.subject: Mid-Mountain House

refs.q: it grew cold as the sun got low; though it was yet summer

records.statement: Cold at sunset even in summer near the House.
records.subject: (unnamed) great snowy mountain

refs.q: save for wide shields which they bore, were but evilly armed, mostly in skins of beasts

records.statement: Wild men are poorly armed, mostly in beast-skins, with wide shields, weak bows, axes, malls and spears; lithe and strong but not tall.
records.subject: Strong-thieves of the mountains

refs.q: they were three-score and two all told, but of these but a score of men-at-arms besides Ralph, and Clement

records.statement: 62 in all: a score of men-at-arms besides Ralph and Clement, chapmen (three old), lads, many archers.
records.subject: Clement's eastward company

refs.q: St. Agnes for the Mercers!

records.statement: War-cries invoke guild saints: "St. Agnes for the Mercers!" and "St. Christopher to aid!"
records.subject: Clement's eastward company

refs.q: no man of the peopled parts would be so hardy as to fall upon the Chapmen

records.statement: Merchants show their banners in the peopled lands, where no one dares attack chapmen they depend on.
records.subject: (unnamed) eastern foothills

refs.q: if thou beat me, save in hot blood, I shall put a knife into thee when I may

records.statement: He warns he will knife his master if beaten except in hot blood.
records.subject: Bull Shockhead

refs.q: Forsooth down there evil they be, and unkinsome

records.statement: He calls the lowland folk evil and unkind.
records.subject: Bull Shockhead

refs.q: And are all men your foemen who pass through these mountains?

records.statement: The mountain folk count all passers-by as foes except kin and known friends.
records.subject: (unnamed) kindred of the Bull

refs.q: they know not the name of their mother's mother, nor have heard one word of the beginner of their kindred

records.statement: Bull values lineage and despises kinless chapmen and their hired swordsmen.
records.subject: (unnamed) kindred of the Bull

refs.q: this life of a bought thrall is not such an exceeding evil life

records.statement: He says a bought thrall's life is not so bad; some have thralls of their own under them.
records.subject: Bull Shockhead

refs.q: there was no weeping or screeching in her, but patience rather and quietness, and intent to bear all and live

records.statement: Captured, she showed no weeping but patience and intent to endure.
records.subject: Ursula

refs.q: they had been cut down lest they should serve as cover to strong-thieves or folk assailing the town

records.statement: Trees and thickets near the walls are cut down to deny cover to thieves and attackers.
records.subject: Cheaping Knowe

refs.q: there were men and women there, yea, and babes also, hanging on gibbets and thrust through with sharp pales

records.statement: Men, women and babes hang on gibbets or are impaled on the castle hill; townsfolk will not say why.
records.subject: (unnamed) tyrant of Cheaping Knowe

refs.q: he will not meddle, lest there be an end of chaffer in the town

records.statement: The founder meant all to thrive, but there are many poor and few wealthy.

records.statement: Many are ragged and beg from the chapmen; others are richly dressed.

records.statement: The old woman speaks a language Ralph does not know.

records.statement: The woodman has only wild fowl to offer.

records.statement: He deliberately keeps the land toward Goldburg barren so it cannot feed a host against him.

records.statement: By the war-arrow he can raise about a thousand rough men from the deserts.

records.subject: Ursula

records.statement: She swears by the beads they must live as long as they may.

records.subject: Burg of the Four Friths

records.statement: Ralph's aim: return to Upmeads, guard it from waste and fire, keep war away, raise children, lie with his fathers in St. Laurence.
records.subject: Ralph

records.statement: The Sage foretells that what Ursula lost she shall find again, and neither will have shame in life nor fear in death.

records.statement: Travellers should go through the rock-sea only where the token is seen, going or returning.

records.statement: Its kindling is held to bode ill to the lord of Utterbol.

refs.q: there is many a prowling beast about, as bear and lynx and lion

records.statement: Harts, wild bulls and goats graze; bears, lynxes and lions prowl.

records.statement: He has not dared use the Well's gift for fear of abusing it.

records.statement: Light in the pass is little better than twilight at best.
records.subject: (unnamed) pass of the Fighting Man

records.statement: Chestnuts are dried and ground into meal for bread; walnuts gathered; venison plentiful.

records.statement: Bears come down to feed on nuts and berries; Ralph kills two great bears.
records.subject: Vale of Sweet Chestnuts

refs.q: which Ursula fell to work on deftly, for she knew all the craft of needlework

records.statement: Ursula knows all needlework and makes fur clothing and bedding.
records.subject: Ursula

records.statement: They arrive in autumn as the days shorten.
records.subject: Vale of Sweet Chestnuts

records.statement: Ursula had parents, a sister who died, and a brother; several suitors.

refs.q: she also was country-bred, of a lineage of field-folk

records.statement: Ursula is country-bred, of a lineage of field-folk.
records.subject: Ursula

records.statement: Frost, snow and prodigious winds in winter; Candlemas thaw floods the valley.
records.subject: Vale of Sweet Chestnuts

refs.q: the waters were thronged with fowl, as mallard and teal and coots

records.statement: Spring floods bring mallard, teal and coots; spring flowers (snowdrop, celandine, blackthorn, Lent-lilies) and birds.
records.subject: Vale of Sweet Chestnuts

records.statement: Horses haul supplies on bough sledges.

records.statement: Ralph resolves to return and kill the Lord of Utterbol; Ursula will share his fate.

refs.q: held in chase by a huge bear as big as a bullock

records.statement: Bears are fierce in these wastes; a he-bear "as big as a bullock" chases Ursula.
records.subject: Vale of Sweet Chestnuts

records.statement: Ursula wants witnesses at the wedding, as in the old heathen custom of a public wedding.
records.subject: Ursula

records.statement: Ursula believes the homeward road's perils will overcome them if they have not drunk.

records.statement: They ride and pack oxen.

records.statement: Green-stone-bladed axes and strong bows; no armour.
records.subject: Innocent Folk

refs.q: raiment of fine white wool for those twain, broidered in strange but beauteous fashion with the feathers of bright-hued birds

records.statement: White wool clothing; wedding robes embroidered with bright bird feathers.
records.subject: Innocent Folk

refs.q: such a bower as we build for our own folk on the night of the wedding

records.statement: They build a wattled bower for a wedding night, as for their own folk.
records.subject: Innocent Folk

refs.q: we hear not that it shall be the worse for you in any wise that ye shall become one flesh

records.statement: The elder says wedding does not harm the quest.

records.statement: It is many years since they found seekers at the cave.
records.subject: Innocent Folk

refs.q: there was wine there in well-hooped kegs, and wooden cups fairly carven

records.statement: They bring meal, wine in hooped kegs and carved wooden cups.
records.subject: Innocent Folk

refs.q: Yet was there naught of filth or famine, nor any poverty or misery

records.statement: No filth, famine, poverty or misery; merry, well-fed folk; the town has no war defences.
records.subject: Innocent Folk

refs.q: they set them down on a dais as though they had been kings, or rather gods

records.statement: They treat the seekers with reverence, as kings or gods.
records.subject: Innocent Folk

records.statement: Corn, vineyards, sheep and cattle.

records.statement: They have never seen horses; the elder saw one knight on horseback in his youth.

records.statement: Guests are bathed, robed in fine white wool, crowned with flowers and feasted with songs of earth's fairness.

records.subject: Sage of Swevenham

records.statement: The Well makes one thrive and live through generations but not for ever; the gods gave death lest men weary of life.
records.subject: Well at the World's End

records.statement: They know no sickness, pestilence or war, and desire nothing hard to attain.
records.subject: Innocent Folk

records.statement: They fear that a few who drank would become earthly gods and tyrannise the rest.
records.subject: Innocent Folk

records.statement: Care of the quest is hereditary in the elder's family.
records.subject: Innocent Folk

records.statement: Ralph marks rocks and mounds in the waste for the return.

records.statement: They call Ralph and Ursula "the Heavenly Folk" and speak of "the Gods".

records.statement: Wild creatures there know no man and are tame; a robin perches on Ursula's wrist.

records.statement: Seekers must cross the ridges at their highest to avoid a maze of hills leading nowhere.

records.statement: The dead came over a long time, one, two or three at a time.

records.statement: None of the desert's dead wear the seekers' beads.

records.statement: The dead all wear the same grin, "as though they had died in pain, and yet beguiled".

records.subject: Ralph

records.statement: No way-token is near the pool, unlike at other watering-places.
records.subject: Thirsty Desert

records.statement: The tree is hung with blazoned shields, helms, swords, spears, axes and hauberks of many unknown fashions.

records.statement: The salt crust ends and dwarf willow and willow-herb appear near water.

records.statement: A far-off roar like many waters is heard (the sea).

records.statement: The Sage and his books taught that seekers must reach the verge of the earth-girdling Ocean-Sea.
records.subject: Ocean Sea

records.subject: Well at the World's End

refs.q: he felt that the water was sweet without any saltness of the sea
a sweet weariness began to steal over them

records.statement: The water is sweet, not salt; drinking brings a sweet weariness and sleep.

refs.q: he put the cup into the ambrye, and shut it up again

records.statement: Seekers drink from the cup in the hallowed raiment from the House of the Sorceress, then return it to its cupboard.

records.statement: The pound is of huge ashlar; water overflows its lip in a thin veil.

records.statement: Large tides: half a mile of sand bared at ebb.
records.subject: Ocean Sea

In sooth here is no mark nor blemish

records.statement: Deer, thrushes and hares there are tame and come to the hand.

records.statement: Ursula says no one at Utterbol would have avenged Gandolf, but all feared him.

records.statement: He made atonement to the slain lord's widow by marrying her.

records.subject: Bull Shockhead

records.statement: The Lord plans a cheaping town in the Dale of the Tower and tillage of the wilderness beyond.
records.subject: Dale of the Tower

records.statement: Ralph's oath: go home to his kindred and refuse help to none on the road.

refs.q: gems and fair women were what the late lord had lusted for the most

records.statement: Gandolf lusted most for gems and fair women.
records.subject: Gandolf

refs.q: being but young of years

records.statement: Bull is young.
records.subject: Bull Shockhead

records.statement: Bull has a gift that wild things love and obey him: mice, birds, squirrels, hares, fierce hounds, and a lion.
records.subject: Bull Shockhead

refs.q: Yea, a very paradise; yet the dwellers therein as if it were hell

records.statement: Utterness is poor and wretched; the House of Utterbol is a paradise where folk lived as in hell.
records.subject: Utterbol

records.statement: All feared and hated him; habit, fear and doubt protected him; he was thought a devil.

refs.q: thou knowest I can some skill with the fiddle and song, so I betook myself to that craft

records.statement: Bull earned his living as a fiddler and singer at merry-makings in Goldburg.
records.subject: Bull Shockhead

refs.q: he made thy friend Agatha pay for her under pretence of wringing a true tale out of her

records.statement: Gandolf blamed the Lady for Ursula's flight but feared to harm her, so he tortured Agatha.
records.subject: Gandolf

refs.q: she had got it spread abroad that she was cunning in sorcery, and that her spell would not end when her life ended

records.statement: Agatha protected herself by spreading that she was a sorceress whose spell would outlive her and curse her killer.
records.subject: Agatha

records.statement: Redhead says Bull often speaks of his kin and long descent.
records.subject: Bull Shockhead

records.statement: The Sage foretells Bull's oath will bring gain to him and Ralph's friends.

records.statement: Redhead is valiant, brisk, grateful, trusty and merry despite rough manners.
records.subject: Redhead

refs.q: with a great screeching yell cast their spears into the rest

records.statement: Black armour and black horses; bowmen from a thicket; a screeching yell as they charge.
records.subject: Black Riders

records.statement: Utterbol's men take no prisoners from raiders; sixteen enemies slain, four of theirs.
records.subject: Bull Shockhead

refs.q: naught save a fowler of the waste, or a peat-cutter, who stood to look on the men-at-arms going by, and made obeisance to the token of Utterbol

records.statement: Fowlers and peat-cutters in the waste bow to Utterbol's token.
records.subject: Bull Shockhead

refs.q: steel kept out steel: I have no scratch or point or edge on me

records.statement: Ursula wears a hauberk and steel coif in battle; a javelin fails to pierce it.
records.subject: Ursula

refs.q: That which trieth a man, is to fight and overcome, and straight have to fight with fresh foemen

records.statement: Redhead says the true test of a man is fighting fresh foes one after another until longing for night or death.
records.subject: Redhead

records.statement: Hiring men-at-arms requires the Clerk of the Porte's licence; the King need not be seen except by traders or soldiers.

refs.q: There is the King's wedded wife, but her they call not Queen, but Lady

records.statement: The King's wife is called Lady, not Queen.
records.subject: Goldburg

refs.q: many deemed that though her lineage was known by seeming, yet she was of the fairy

records.statement: Some think the Queen was of the fairy and needed no steed; her women think she killed herself for love.
records.subject: Queen of Goldburg

refs.q: in the early spring, somewhat more than a year ago that is, one morning when folk arose, the Queen's place was empty

records.statement: She vanished in early spring a little over a year before.
records.subject: Queen of Goldburg

refs.q: a little before there had been a great overthrow of the wild men of those mountains at the hands of the men of Goldburg and the Chapmen

records.statement: Goldburg and the chapmen lately routed the mountain wild men.
records.subject: Goldburg

refs.q: handless men, fettered, dragging themselves about, and folk hung up before chapmen's booths, and whipping-cheer, and the pillar

records.statement: Cruel justice: handless men in fetters, folk hung before booths, whippings, the pillar.
records.subject: (unnamed) King of Cheaping Knowe

records.statement: When Ralph declares he has drunk of the Well, the hall falls back and bows.

refs.q: who were, so to say, his barons, though they were not barons of lineage, but masterful men who were wise to do his bidding

records.statement: His captains are self-made, not barons of lineage.
records.subject: (unnamed) King of Cheaping Knowe

refs.q: bought a goodly gift of silver vessel and fine cloth for the King of Cheaping Knowe

records.statement: Ralph brings silver vessels and fine cloth as a gift to buy the King's goodwill.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: this tyrant wages many a spy

records.statement: He keeps many spies.
records.subject: (unnamed) King of Cheaping Knowe

records.statement: They ambush from woods with arrows and casting-spears, and bellow like cattle as a clan signal.

records.statement: They leave enemy dead for wolves, lynxes, ravens and kites.

refs.q: The Duke and all his men were afoot, but they went easily and swiftly, as wolves trot

records.statement: They go on foot, swiftly, "as wolves trot".
records.subject: Folk of the Fells

refs.q: whereas if a man were their friend he could scarce be enough their friend, and if he were their foe, they could never be fierce enough with him

records.statement: They are boundless friends and implacable foes.
records.subject: Folk of the Fells

refs.q: we have been minded to stop everything bigger than a cur-dog that might seek to pass by us

records.statement: They had resolved to stop all traffic through the mountains while the cruel King lived.
records.subject: Folk of the Fells

refs.q: Home, home to Upmeads!

records.statement: Ralph's war-cry: "Home, home to Upmeads!"
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: strong men, but not high of stature, black-haired, with blue or grey eyes, cheerful of countenance, and of many words

records.statement: Strong, not tall, black-haired, blue- or grey-eyed, cheerful and talkative; women comely and kind but refusing strangers' caresses.

records.statement: They keep no thralls: adult captives are sold, killed or ransomed; captured children are sometimes adopted.
records.subject: Folk of the Fells

records.statement: Their gods are their forefathers; adopted children are made kin with prayers and worship.
records.subject: Folk of the Fells

refs.q: they showed the wayfarers their manner of hunting, both of the hart and the boar, and of wild bulls also

records.statement: They hunt hart, boar and wild bulls in the mountains.
records.subject: Folk of the Fells

refs.q: the way thither was well defensible were foemen to try it

records.statement: Its defence is concealment and defensible approaches.

records.statement: Ursula fears that among the barons and lineages of the west she will be scorned as a yeoman's daughter.
records.subject: Ursula

records.statement: Ralph swears on his sword that if his kin do not honour Ursula he will leave his land and found a new kindred with her.
records.subject: Ralph

records.statement: Ursula says he is now fit for the Kaiser's throne.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: the little cloud of dust about us two in the late spring weather

records.statement: Late spring, dusty dry highway.
records.subject: (unnamed) plain west of the mountains

refs.q: This man shall make old bones

records.statement: The Sage reads palms and foretells Michael's long life.
records.subject: Sage of Swevenham

refs.q: somewhat like am I yet to myself of forty years ago

records.statement: Richard remembers him from forty years ago looking much the same.
records.subject: Sage of Swevenham

refs.q: he speaketh as a Friend of the Well, and wotteth more of far-off tidings than even this wise man of many years

records.statement: Ursula says Ralph as a Friend of the Well knows far-off tidings better than the Sage; Ralph senses danger at Upmeads.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: Many were glad of his death, and few sorrowed for it

records.statement: Whitwall made peace after Walter the Black's death; Richard says many were glad, for he was a cruel tyrant.
records.subject: Whitwall

refs.q: now hast thou wedded into the World of living men, and not to a dream of the Land of Fairy

records.statement: Richard is relieved Ralph married into "the World of living men" and not a fairy dream.
records.subject: Richard the Red

refs.q: on a Saturday of latter May, It was a market-day

records.statement: Market day on Saturday in latter May.
records.subject: Whitwall

refs.q: one rumour sayeth, and none denieth it, that the old fierceness and stout headstrong mood of the Burg is broken down

records.statement: Rumour says the Burg's old fierceness is broken and folk there live in peace.
records.subject: Burg of the Four Friths

refs.q: our chapmen but seldom go there

records.statement: Whitwall chapmen seldom go to the Burg and little news comes from it.
records.subject: Burg of the Four Friths

refs.q: laid him down there beside the howe which Ralph had erewhile heaped over the Lady; and now over him also they heaped stones

records.statement: He asks to be buried beside the Lady; they lay him in the cave beside her cairn under stones.
records.subject: Captain of the Dry Tree

refs.q: Now is the riddle areded of the wild-man and the mighty giant that haunted these passes

records.statement: Richard knew him in old fights and says he always won; he haunted these passes as a wild giant.
records.subject: Captain of the Dry Tree

refs.q: The last time!

records.statement: His last words complete the count: "The last time!"
records.subject: Captain of the Dry Tree

refs.q: They saw but few houses, and those small and poor

records.statement: Few, poor houses; shepherds short of speech.
records.subject: (unnamed) sheep downs by the Swelling Flood

refs.q: give guesting therein to any wandering knight or pilgrim, or honest goodman, who shall come to you

records.statement: The folk ask Ralph to be lord in the Lady's memory; he asks only castle-keeping and hospitality to travellers.
records.subject: Plain of Abundance

refs.q: never did she lay tax or tale on us, and whiles she would give us of her store

records.statement: She never taxed them and gave from her store; they think harvests have been poorer since she stopped coming.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: where she set her feet the grass grew greener

records.statement: Folk say grass grew greener and flowers fairer where she walked.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: for the wood was to them as a wall

records.statement: The wood is a wall to them; they would send a Thorn brother as messenger.
records.subject: yeomen of Abundance

refs.q: bread in baskets, and cheeses both fresh and old, and honey, and wood-strawberries

records.statement: The feast: bread, cheeses, honey, wild strawberries, eggs, skewered roast lamb, salad, wine and orchard cider.
records.subject: yeomen of Abundance

refs.q: by night and cloud fell upon these faineants of the Burg, and won them good cheap

records.statement: Grieving Dry Tree riders ambushed a Burg host with Wheat-wearer captives and freed the women.
records.subject: Burg of the Four Friths

refs.q: our land is ill-furnished of carles, so that we women, high and low, go afield and do many things

records.statement: With few men left, Wheat-wearer women do fieldwork and crafts; they proved strong and quick at arms.
records.subject: Wheat-wearers

refs.q: they fled before the spears had met, and in such evil order that the gates could not be shut

records.statement: The Burg's men fled at the push; the gates could not be shut; the town fell in an hour.
records.subject: Burg of the Four Friths

refs.q: of whom there were some two thousand alive after the Burg was taken

records.statement: Freed Wheat-wearer thrall women came out in green and garlands; there were about two thousand former bondwomen.
records.subject: Burg of the Four Friths

refs.q: now a mixed folk are dwelling in the Burg

records.statement: The Burg is now a mixed folk (freed thralls, Wheat-wearers, Dry Tree men, incomers) under a Dry Tree captain, well ordered for defence.
records.subject: Burg of the Four Friths

refs.q: two or three carles and a dozen of women dwell now in the halls and chambers of the Scaur

records.statement: The Scaur holds only two or three carles and a dozen women.
records.subject: Hampton under Scaur

refs.q: the day shall come meseemeth when folk shall call on thee to lead the hunt after these famished wolves

records.statement: Roger expects the expelled Burgers to raid peaceful folk and Ralph to be called to hunt them.
records.subject: (unnamed) expelled Burgers

refs.q: she it was who ordained this Ursula to be Ralph's bedmate

records.statement: The Sage says the Lady ordained Ursula as Ralph's mate and fellow Friend of the Well.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: the women like to those fair thralls whom he had seen that other time, saving that they were not clad so wantonly, however gaily

records.statement: Townsfolk now walk outside the gates merrily; the town is gayer; women dress gaily but less wantonly than the former thralls.
records.subject: Burg of the Four Friths

refs.q: they saw a watchman on each of the high towers of the south gate

records.statement: Few carry weapons in the fields, but helms gleam on the walls and watchmen are on the South Gate towers.
records.subject: Burg of the Four Friths

records.context: dialogue:maiden of the Flower de Luce

refs.q: If the Burgers come back, they will find them upon the walls who have already chaced them

records.statement: The women of the new Burg helped chase the Burgers and will hold the walls.
records.subject: Burg of the Four Friths

refs.q: the masons and builders had begun on the master church to make it fairer and bigger

records.statement: The master church is being enlarged and beautified.
records.subject: Burg of the Four Friths

refs.q: rumour goes that there are alien riders come into the lands of Higham

records.statement: Rumour says alien riders have come into Higham's lands.
records.subject: Higham-on-the-Way

records.context: dialogue:maiden of the Flower de Luce

refs.q: already rumour was abroad that they were in the Burg who had drunk of the Water of the Well at the World's End

records.statement: Rumour already says they have drunk of the Well.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: they were threescore save five, besides Roger and the way-farers

records.statement: Ralph's first band: fifty-five Dry Tree champions plus Roger and the travellers.
records.subject: Fellowship of the Dry Tree

refs.q: By the hilts and the blade, by the point and the edge, we swear

records.statement: The Dry Tree swears on a sword's blade, hilt, point and edge, kissing it.
records.subject: Fellowship of the Dry Tree

records.context: dialogue:new Captain of the Dry Tree

refs.q: five hundred good men of the Wheat-wearers, men who have not learned the feat of arms a-horseback, are coming through the woods hither

records.statement: Five hundred Wheat-wearer foot are coming to garrison the Scaur and bring remounts.
records.subject: Burg of the Four Friths

refs.q: May God bless this House and the abode of the valiant, and the shelter of the hapless

records.statement: Roger says the Duke brought the cast-out Lady into the hall in his scarlet cloak, where she blessed the house as the abode of the valiant and shelter of the hapless.
records.subject: Lady of Abundance

refs.q: A rumour there is that she walketh

records.statement: A rumour says her ghost walks in the Scaur's hall.
records.subject: (unnamed) old Queen of the Dry Tree

refs.q: the evil hag with hair like a grey she-bear

records.statement: Ursula was taken by women of the thorp, mishandled, and condemned in the hall by the old Queen ("hair like a grey she-bear").
records.subject: Ursula

refs.q: there were strong barriers before it, and men-at-arms within them, as though they were looking for an onfall

records.statement: Higham has barriers before its gate and expects attack.
records.subject: Higham-on-the-Way

refs.q: Wilt thou then lodge thy company of strong-thieves with honest men?

records.statement: Higham's men still regard the Dry Tree as strong-thieves.
records.subject: Fellowship of the Dry Tree

refs.q: all three of them bare-headed with their swords in the sheaths; and Stephen moreover bearing a white cloth on a truncheon

records.statement: Ralph approaches bareheaded with a white cloth on a truncheon to show peaceful intent.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: many of his manors had castles and strong-houses on them

records.statement: Before the war the Abbot was mighty: Higham was well manned, many manors had castles and strong-houses, and yeomen answered the gathering horn.
records.subject: St. Mary's of Higham

refs.q: some year and a half ago, the Abbot had debate with the Westland Barons

records.statement: About a year and a half ago the Abbot led his host against the Westland Barons in armour and was overthrown and taken.
records.subject: St. Mary's of Higham
records.when: about a year and a half before

refs.q: the lands of Higham are half ruined

records.statement: The Westlanders besieged Higham and failed, but took most of the Abbot's castles and strong-houses, burned some, garrisoned others, and drove off chattels and people.
records.subject: Higham-on-the-Way

refs.q: they are grown sour and churlish

records.statement: The monks will not let their men ride abroad, so the garrison is cooped up and has grown sour and churlish.
records.subject: Higham-on-the-Way

refs.q: those Champions have made covenant with the devil to come to their above whensoever they be not more than one to five

records.statement: Higham's monks say the Dry Tree has a covenant with the devil to win unless outnumbered more than five to one, and that devils walk among them as men and women.
records.subject: Fellowship of the Dry Tree

refs.q: whom the warriors of the town had sent out cautiously to see if they might catch a few men for their ranks

records.statement: Higham's sergeants press captured wood-thieves into service, offering them the gallows or the Church.
records.subject: St. Mary's of Higham

refs.q: we be a poor unwalled people

records.statement: The thorp is a poor unwalled people; its elders meet newcomers cap in hand by a fire at the street cross.
records.subject: Garton

refs.q: lodging the more part of them in a big barn on the western outskirt of the thorp

records.statement: The riders lodge in a big barn on the western outskirt, the side from which attack is expected.
records.subject: Garton

refs.q: to heed well that he hurt no man, or let fire get into any house or roof

records.statement: Ralph pays good silver for victual and forbids hurting folk or setting fire to roofs.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: ever it fell out according to her spaedom

records.statement: Martha's foretellings have always come true; she foresees Ralph's road, the mote at Bear Castle and the host at Wulstead.
records.subject: Martha

refs.q: there shall come to our helping one from afar, whose home is anigh

records.statement: An old tale says a helper from afar whose home is near, a stripling and a great man, a runaway and conqueror, will come in their need.
records.subject: shepherds of the Downs

refs.q: whereas our houses be uncostly and that we move about easily from one hill-side to another

records.statement: The shepherds are few, live in cheap houses, move from hillside to hillside, and every grown man can handle weapons.
records.subject: shepherds of the Downs

refs.q: there have been tokens on earth and in the heavens

records.statement: Tokens on earth and in the heavens have stirred the scattered shepherds to meet in arms.
records.subject: shepherds of the Downs

refs.q: there I shall give the token of the four fires which erewhile a good man of the Shepherds bade me if I were in need

records.statement: Four fires at Bear Castle are the shepherds' call for help, as one of them told Ralph.
records.subject: shepherds of the Downs

refs.q: two score and six (as they counted them afterward)

records.statement: Ralph's band surprises forty-six Burgers; half are slain at once and the rest yield.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: Two thousand, lord

records.statement: Two thousand Burgers are marching on Upmeads, with somewhat more than a thousand expected from Higham-land.
records.subject: (unnamed) expelled Burgers

refs.q: do thy folk in these strongholds know of your purpose of falling upon Upmeads?

records.statement: The Burgers in the southern strongholds do not know of the march on Upmeads.
records.subject: (unnamed) expelled Burgers

refs.q: the Upmeads carles, though they be not many, are strong and dauntless

records.statement: The Woodmen say the Upmeads carles are few but strong and dauntless.
records.subject: outlaws of the Wood Debateable

refs.q: But I have given life to these others, and so it must be held to

records.statement: Ralph swears quarter by the sword blade and holds to it after a captive's murder.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: rose up into the air a column of smoke intermingled with fire from each of the four corners

records.statement: At the mote, smoke and fire rise from each of the four corners of Bear Castle.
records.subject: shepherds of the Downs

refs.q: numbered twenty and three all told

records.statement: Twenty-three Garton spearmen join Ralph.
records.subject: Garton

refs.q: There arose a hum of assent from the Shepherds as he spoke and men clashed their weapons together

records.statement: The mote is hallowed by an Elder with set words; assent is shown by humming and clashing weapons.
records.subject: shepherds of the Downs

refs.q: wilt thou be our Captain as an alien and a hireling, or as a brother?

records.statement: The shepherds choose a war Captain and ask whether he serves as an alien hireling or as a brother.
records.subject: shepherds of the Downs

refs.q: yet have we wherewithal to wage you

records.statement: The shepherds offer to pay allies for war, though unhoused or ill-housed.
records.subject: shepherds of the Downs

refs.q: they were told over and made five hundred and fifty and four

records.statement: Ralph's host: 150 Dry Tree champions (besides Stephen and Roger), 22 of Garton, 377 shepherds (about 80 bowmen, the rest with glaives, spears and staff-weapons), 554 in all.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: There was not much armour of defence amongst them

records.statement: The shepherds have little defensive armour but are stark and doughty.
records.subject: shepherds of the Downs

refs.q: appointed them leaders of tens and hundreds with the help of Giles

records.statement: Ralph appoints leaders of tens and hundreds.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: certain women brought victual and drink to them, and served the strangers first

records.statement: After the mote, women bring food and drink and serve the strangers first.
records.subject: shepherds of the Downs

refs.q: came the sound of the blowing of great horns, and the spears thickened in the towers

records.statement: Wulstead, formerly unwalled, is now fenced with pales and gate towers, manned with spears and horns.
records.subject: Wulstead

refs.q: I deem there be some two thousand devils

records.statement: Clement reckons about two thousand Burgers beyond Wulstead.
records.subject: (unnamed) expelled Burgers

refs.q: they have fled, with many another, women and children and old men

records.statement: Upmeads' women, children and old men have fled to Wulstead; the carles hold the High House under Nicholas.
records.subject: Upmeads

refs.q: which shall not suffer that a Friend of the Well shall be hurt

records.statement: The Sage says no arrow will be suffered to hurt a Friend of the Well.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: whereas thou didst bring him safe through the mountains unto Goldburg

records.statement: Ursula credits Clement with saving her, since he brought Ralph through the mountains to Goldburg.
records.subject: Ursula

refs.q: she is upon the north gate in war-gear

records.statement: Katherine stands on Wulstead's north gate in war-gear; Wulstead is too short of folk to spare her.
records.subject: Dame Katherine

refs.q: It was a fair house with a church but just finished

records.statement: The canons' church is newly finished, with new white pinnacles, a cross on the eastern gable, and painted windows.
records.subject: House of Black Canons of Wulstead

refs.q: It is told amongst us that that word is but another way of saying earl and that it meaneth a man

records.statement: Ursula says "churl" is another way of saying "earl" and means a man; her kin remember their forefathers though they labour afield.
records.subject: Geirings

refs.q: my business is to be a king, or a kinglet rather

records.statement: Peter calls himself a king, or rather a kinglet, and says Upmeads has failed them.
records.subject: King Peter

refs.q: who have heard not tidings of their best beloved son for two years well nigh

records.statement: Ralph's parents had no news of him for nearly two years.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: of the eldest, who meseems was born with a long head, we hear that he is thriving

records.statement: King Peter hears that his eldest son is thriving and has grown great.
records.subject: Blaise

refs.q: they had no inkling of the Shepherds or the Dry Tree coming against them

records.statement: The Burgers skirmished with Nicholas at the High House without gain. They know nothing of the Shepherds or the Dry Tree and await their Higham-land folk.
records.subject: (unnamed) expelled Burgers

refs.q: nor would they burn either the High House or the other steadings

records.statement: The Burgers will not burn the High House or steadings, meaning to keep them for their own.
records.subject: (unnamed) expelled Burgers

refs.q: so young in years, being so old in the wisdom of war

records.statement: Ralph briefs all leaders on how footmen and horsemen shall stand and fall on, and they marvel at his wisdom in war.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: as for her drinking of the Well at the World's End, it is not so

records.statement: Katherine looks younger than her age; Clement says she has not drunk of the Well, but such wise women wear well.
records.subject: Dame Katherine

refs.q: This pair of beads shall one day lead a man unto the Well at the World's End, but no woman

records.statement: The beads lead a man to the Well at the World's End but not a woman; in a woman's hands they are only a token; others like them exist.
records.subject: Dame Katherine's necklace

refs.q: only he shall not be of thine own blood

records.statement: They must go to a man the bearer loves well, not of her blood, in his greatest need; failing brings harm.
records.subject: Dame Katherine's necklace

refs.q: this meeting betwixt us is not by chance-hap, but of my bringing about

records.statement: She drew Katherine to her deliberately, foretold Valerius's sudden departure, and expected to die soon.
records.subject: (unnamed) Wise Woman of Sarras

refs.q: I was wishful to see the ways of the world even at the risk of being thrust out of the world

records.statement: As a young wife Katherine travelled with Clement on perilous journeys to see the world.
records.subject: Dame Katherine

refs.q: where the world endeth the clouds begin

records.statement: Clement scoffed at the Well, saying that where the world ends the clouds begin.
records.subject: Clement Chapman

refs.q: four trumpets, which were sounding in the four quarters of the town

records.statement: Four trumpets in the four quarters of the town blow the muster at dawn.
records.subject: Wulstead

refs.q: they were a thousand and four score and three

records.statement: Ralph's host at Wulstead is 1,083 men: his company, Wulstead's men, and Upmeads refugees, mostly old men and lads.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: for the sun to shine on, so that I may be seen from far

records.statement: Ralph fights afoot without armour save a sallet, bearing the guisarme, so as to be seen from afar.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: Thou biddest us wisdom of war; let them have the hill against them

records.statement: Ralph's council chooses to await the attack on the hillside, keeping the slope against the enemy; the Dry Tree stay horsed to pursue.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: they came in two battles straight across the meadow

records.statement: The Burgers come in two battles: riders against the Dry Tree, and a great foot battle with horse in its rear against the Shepherds.
records.subject: (unnamed) expelled Burgers

refs.q: Then befell a marvel

records.statement: When Ralph stands on the mound and cries "Home to Upmeads", every foe who looks on him throws down his weapons and flees in terror.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: of thy Shepherds and the other footmen is not one slain, and but some five hurt

records.statement: Losses: no Shepherd or footman slain, about five hurt; the Dry Tree lose three slain and about fifteen hurt, Hugh among them but not badly.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: or long I shall clear the said wood of all strong-thieves

records.statement: About two hundred Burger prisoners are stripped and driven into the Wood Debateable; Ralph vows to clear the wood of strong-thieves.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: the banner of the fruited tree hanging forth from the topmost tower thereof

records.statement: The High House flies the banner of the fruited tree from its topmost tower.
records.subject: High House of Upmeads

refs.q: Better the ghosts of robbers in our fields by night, than the over-burdened hapless thrall by day

records.statement: Ralph says the ghosts of robbers by night are better than thralls, scourged women and ruined children by day.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: the days will presently find deeds for thee, and thou wilt be riding into peril, and coming safe from out of it

records.statement: Katherine says she looked for no other tidings and foresees that the days will find deeds and perils for Ralph.
records.subject: Dame Katherine

refs.q: already were the Upmeads carles at work digging trenches wherein to bury them

records.statement: The Upmeads carles dig trenches to bury the slain robbers.
records.subject: Upmeads

refs.q: my day is done, my dear

records.statement: King Peter remarks that his day is done as Ralph grows masterful.
records.subject: King Peter

refs.q: the Upmeads carles and queans had taken the more part of the host to their houses

records.statement: The Upmeads folk take most of the host into their houses, which the host has saved from fire and sword.
records.subject: Upmeads

refs.q: the cupbearers, being so bidden before, brought it last of all to King Peter

records.statement: The great cup, the River of Upmeads, is brought last to the king for his proclamation.
records.subject: High House of Upmeads

refs.q: then shall the vassals swear to him according to ancient custom

records.statement: A king of Upmeads swears oaths in St. Laurence's choir before mass; the vassals then swear by ancient custom.
records.subject: Upmeads

refs.q: of all the kindred he is meetest to sit therein so long as he liveth

records.statement: King Peter abdicates for Ralph as the meetest of the kindred, not for love alone.
records.subject: Upmeads

refs.q: clad in the daintiest of her woman's gear of the web of Goldburg

records.statement: Ursula wears gear of the web (cloth) of Goldburg.
records.subject: Ursula

refs.q: it has been deemed not unlike that from this monk's writing has come the more part of the tale above told

records.statement: The tale was written by a monk of St. Austin's at Wulstead as Ralph told it to the Prior.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: oft forsooth the very sound of his name and rumour of his coming stayed the march of hosts

records.statement: Ralph rules justly, delivers other lands and towns, and his name alone stops hosts.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: cleansed the Wood Perilous of all strong-thieves and reivers

records.statement: Ralph clears the Wood Perilous of strong-thieves so that its glades are as safe as a town street.
records.subject: Wood Perilous

refs.q: rooted out the last of the Burg-devils

records.statement: Ralph clears the Wood Debateable and roots out the last Burg-devils.
records.subject: Wood Debateable

refs.q: Ever was he true captain and brother to the Shepherd-folk

records.statement: Ralph remains their captain and brother and helps them in scarcity.
records.subject: shepherds of the Downs

refs.q: he went into the castle there as into a holy place

records.statement: Ralph and Ursula visit yearly; Ralph enters the castle as a holy place to honour the Lady.
records.subject: Plain of Abundance

refs.q: he was to all men's eyes in the very blossom of his age

records.statement: Ralph and Ursula never appear to age and die exceedingly old, as in the blossom of their age.
records.subject: Ralph

refs.q: now become a very mighty man and the warder of the peace of the Uttermost lands

records.statement: The Lord of Utterbol becomes a mighty man and warder of the peace of the Uttermost lands.
records.subject: Utterbol
